blocks.content: This chapter opens a new module on how an operating system actually handles input and output efficiently, and interrupts are the foundational mechanism everything else in this module builds on. An interrupt is a signal that lets a hardware device tell the CPU something needs attention right now, without the CPU having to constantly ask.

Understanding interrupts precisely also connects directly back to material already covered earlier in this course, the interrupt handling sequence closely mirrors a context switch, and system calls, covered when discussing fork and exec, are themselves a specific kind of software interrupt.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409604735-761954508.png
1. The Problem Interrupts Solve: Polling

Without interrupts, the only way for a CPU to know when a slow device, a disk, a keyboard, a network card, has finished an operation or has new data ready would be polling: repeatedly checking that device status in a tight loop, over and over, asking are you ready yet.

This is honestly wasteful. A device operation can take a very long time relative to CPU speed, and a CPU stuck polling in a loop the whole time is CPU capacity that could have been doing genuinely useful work elsewhere, sitting completely idle in every practical sense despite technically being busy.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409604735-760199793.png

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: An interrupt lets a device proactively notify the CPU the instant something needs attention, eliminating the need for the CPU to waste cycles repeatedly asking whether anything has changed.
2. The Full Interrupt Handling Sequence

When a device raises an interrupt, a precise, well defined sequence unfolds. The CPU immediately suspends whatever ordinary program instructions it was executing, saves its current state, program counter and register values, so execution can resume exactly where it left off later, and looks up the correct handler for this specific interrupt.

That handler, called an interrupt service routine, ISR, then runs, performing whatever work is actually needed to respond to the event, reading the newly available data, acknowledging the device, or whatever else the specific interrupt calls for. Once the ISR finishes, the CPU restores its previously saved state and resumes the original program exactly where it was interrupted, as if nothing had happened from that program own point of view.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409604735-133869784.png
3. The Interrupt Vector Table

Looking up the correct handler needs to happen extremely quickly, an interrupt is by definition an urgent event. The mechanism that makes this fast is the interrupt vector table, a fixed, pre built array where each interrupt number is simply an index directly into the address of its corresponding handler, no searching required at all.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409604736-147517058.png
4. Hardware Interrupts vs Software Interrupts

Interrupts are not exclusively triggered by physical devices. A hardware interrupt is raised by an actual physical device, a disk finishing a read, a key being pressed, a network packet arriving. A software interrupt is instead raised deliberately by running code itself, using a specific instruction to trigger it intentionally.

The single most important example of a software interrupt, already covered from a different angle earlier in this course, is the system call. When a user program needs a privileged, kernel level operation, it deliberately triggers a software interrupt, trapping into the kernel, which then handles the request through essentially this exact same interrupt mechanism.

5. Maskable vs Non Maskable Interrupts

Not every interrupt can be temporarily blocked. A maskable interrupt can be deliberately, temporarily suppressed by the CPU while it is in the middle of some critical work that genuinely cannot afford to be interrupted right now, the overwhelming majority of ordinary device interrupts fall into this category.

A non maskable interrupt, NMI, cannot be blocked under any circumstances, exactly mirroring SIGKILL uninterruptible nature covered in the signals chapter. NMIs are reserved specifically for the most severe, urgent conditions, a critical hardware failure being the classic example, where ignoring the event even briefly would be genuinely unacceptable.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409609630-498796621.png
6. Interrupt Priority

Multiple interrupts can genuinely arrive close together in time, and not every interrupt deserves equal urgency. Each interrupt line typically carries an assigned priority level, and a sufficiently high priority interrupt is actually allowed to interrupt a lower priority handler that is already running, nesting one interrupt inside another when the situation genuinely calls for it.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409609631-500405188.png
7. The Real Cost: Interrupts Are Not Free
blocks.text: 7. The Real Cost: Interrupts Are Not Free

blocks.content: Handling an interrupt requires the exact same kind of state saving and restoring work a context switch does, covered in full in the context switching chapter, and it carries genuinely comparable real overhead. A very high rate of interrupts arriving in quick succession, sometimes called an interrupt storm, can meaningfully degrade overall system performance purely from this bookkeeping cost, even though each individual interrupt is handled correctly.

items: Assuming interrupts are entirely free, with no real cost, when handling one carries genuine state saving and restoring overhead comparable to a context switch.
Forgetting that a system call is itself a software interrupt, treating it as an entirely separate, unrelated mechanism from the interrupt handling covered in this chapter.
Confusing maskable and non maskable interrupts, and not recognizing the direct parallel to SIGTERM versus SIGKILL from the signals chapter.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to walk through the full interrupt handling sequence from memory, explain precisely why interrupt driven I/O beats polling, and connect system calls directly back to software interrupts, a common, substantive follow up once basic interrupt mechanics have been covered.

Interrupts are what let the CPU stay productive instead of endlessly polling slow devices. The next chapter covers DMA, the mechanism that takes this efficiency one step further by letting devices move data directly without the CPU babysitting every single byte transferred.
